title: Ambrose reading silently (6.3)
hookLine: Augustine is struck that Ambrose reads without moving his lips
tomorrow: can you keep your eyes shut when a whole arena roars?

cards: Three group chats, an inbox, a parent's opinion at dinner, a coach's voicemail. Some weeks are all voices, and your own is the hardest to hear.
Augustine had a week like that, full of questions, and walked into the bishop's house to ask them. The door stood open to anyone. And what was Ambrose doing that Augustine couldn't stop watching?
Reading. His eyes moved down the page. His lips didn't.

teach.b: When Ambrose read, his eyes ran over the pages and his heart searched out the sense, but his voice and tongue were at rest.
Nobody announced visitors in that house, so people would sit in silence a long while, then leave, not wanting to interrupt someone so absorbed. Augustine wonders why he read that way.
Maybe Ambrose didn't want a listener stopping him at a hard passage and using up his little free time. Maybe he was saving a voice that easily grew hoarse.
Whatever the reason, Augustine says, in such a man it was a good one.

And Augustine's own questions had to wait. The bishop's hours went to crowds of people with their troubles, and the few moments left he spent feeding his body or his mind. So what does this give a person in a loud week?
A picture worth keeping: eyes on one page, the heart looking for the sense, the voice at rest. And a surprise.
Augustine got his answers without the private talk he wanted.
On Sundays he heard Ambrose explain the scriptures to everyone, and began to see the Church's teaching wasn't what he'd assumed.

how: Catholics practice slow, prayerful reading of scripture, often called lectio divina: reading a short passage quietly, more than once, and letting it sink in. Some keep a few minutes of silent reading each day.

o: a bishop who refused to preach in public
a bishop reading aloud to the whole city
a bishop reading with eyes and heart, lips still

games.q: the bishop at his book — tap the pairs.

s: Ambrose read silently to keep people away
Augustine didn't know why; he guessed, and said that whatever it was, it was a good reason.
Augustine got long private talks with Ambrose
the bishop's hours went to crowds; Augustine's questions waited.
visitors would sit in silence and leave rather than interrupt
nobody was announced in that house, and nobody wanted to break in.

games.q: your dad has a big decision about his job, and everyone in the family keeps weighing in. what does Ambrose's reading offer him?
o: some quiet with one page, letting the heart look for the sense.
one more round of opinions, until the answer is obvious.
ignore everyone and go with his gut by tonight.
games.why: Ambrose read with his eyes, his heart searching the sense, his voice at rest. Augustine never forgot the picture.

practice: Open a short passage you have nearby, a psalm or a few lines of any book you trust. Read it with your eyes only, slowly, lips at rest, and let your heart look for the sense. When you reach the end, stay there in the quiet.

wordCard.voice: Ambrose reading silently. Eyes on the page, heart searching the sense, voice and tongue at rest: the scene that held Augustine at the bishop's door.

orig.note: Latin, Confessions 6.3: but his voice and tongue were at rest.

carryVoice: Here's your line: reading in silence, where the eyes read and the heart looks for the sense. Until next time.
